courses.title: Start Here
courses.intro: This is where you start. In this course you find your stage, set your target and map out your first seven days. It takes less than an hour. Do it properly and the next twelve weeks make sense.

lessons.title: Welcome to The Method
lessons.big_idea: This is the exact process I used to build my own companies and train the people who now run them. You build the business and you build yourself. One project, ninety days.
talking_points: Welcome. This isn't theory. It's what I did, written down in order, so you can do it too.
I built my own companies and I trained the people who now run them. That's the process you're getting.
A finished business has a definition. You can leave it, sell it, or run it from your phone on the other side of the world, and it holds. Anything less is a job you own.
Ninety days. One course a week. One live call a week. One assignment at the end of every course.
You get four things: the weekly live call, the Classroom, the Vault and the community. Use all four.
Time freedom, location freedom, financial freedom. We design them in from day one. We don't hope for them at the end.
lessons.story: I walked my brother from someone who just wanted to have a company to running one fully remote at six figures a month. This is the same path. [STORY: the moment you realized your process could be taught to someone else]
lessons.action: Block one hour this week and finish every lesson in Course 00 before the next live call.

lessons.title: How to win in here
lessons.big_idea: The people who win in here do the assignments, show their numbers and ask specific questions. Watching isn't doing.
talking_points: Every course ends with one assignment. Do it before you move on. That's where the results are.
Run the weekly rhythm. Monday, post your target for the week and the one number you're moving. Friday, post your wins and your misses. Both count.
Come to the live call with one real question. Thirty minutes of teaching, thirty minutes of your questions. Every call is recorded.
Ask specific questions. 'How do I get clients?' gets you less than 'Here's my offer, my market, and what's broken.'
Show your work. Wins, misses, work in progress. This room runs on real reps.
What's shared here stays here. No pitching. Help people. If you've helped someone, a DM is fine.
lessons.story: [STORY: someone you've coached who moved fast because they did the reps, or one who stalled because they only watched]
lessons.action: Put the live call, a Monday post and a Friday post in your calendar as recurring events for the next twelve weeks.

lessons.title: Find your stage
lessons.big_idea: There are five stages. Pick the one you're actually in, not the one you want to be in. Your stage tells you where to push hardest.
talking_points: Stage 0 is starting from zero. No business yet. Push hardest on Course 02.
Stage 1 is doing it all. You find the work, do the work and chase the invoice. Feast or famine. Push hardest on Courses 03 to 05.
Stage 2 is it runs through you. Real revenue, around ten to thirty thousand a month, and every client needs you. Push hardest on Courses 06 to 09.

Stage 3 is a team, not a machine. People on payroll, around thirty to a hundred thousand a month, and you're still the bottleneck. Push hardest on 09 to 12. Stage 4 is owner, not operator. It runs without you. Push on 13 and 14.
Here's the test. If you stopped working for two weeks, what happens to revenue? Your honest answer tells you your stage.
Most people are one stage behind where they think they are. That's normal. Everyone still runs all ninety days, in order. Your stage just tells you where to spend extra effort.
lessons.story: [STORY: a time you thought you were further along than you were, and what showed you the truth]
lessons.action: Write down your stage, your revenue for each of the last three months, and which of the ten problems you're stuck on: leads, marketing, sales, retention, churn, recruiting, delegation, managing a team, leadership or scaling.

lessons.title: Set your target
lessons.big_idea: A target is three things: a monthly number, a date and the life it pays for. Without all three, it's a wish.
talking_points: Pick one monthly revenue number. Not a range. One number.
Put a date on it. A real date, on a calendar.
Then write down the life it pays for. Where you live, how you spend your week, who you spend it with. That's what gets you through the hard days.
Make it big enough that you'd have to change how you work to hit it. If you can hit it doing what you're doing now, it's not a target.
Make it real enough to work backwards. In Course 11 we turn it into a weekly lead number.
Nobody actually wants a company. They want what it pays for. Start there.
lessons.story: [STORY: the first real target you set, and what happened when you hit it or missed it]
lessons.action: Write your monthly number, your date, and three sentences on the life it pays for. Keep it where you'll see it every morning.

lessons.title: The James Method in ten minutes
lessons.big_idea: Build the business, build yourself. Three moves over ninety days: Money In, The Machine, Step Out. Rich · Fit · Sick runs underneath all of it.
talking_points: My process is simple. You build the business and you build yourself. Not two projects. One.
Move one, days 1 to 30, is Money In. An offer people understand, a steady flow of leads, and you selling it with confidence. Cash coming in every week.
Move two, days 31 to 60, is The Machine. Someone else delivers. Systems, SOPs, a CRM, your first hires. Clients stay, and the work moves without you touching it.
Move three, days 61 to 90, is Step Out. The numbers run on a scoreboard, the team runs the day, and you run the company from your phone, anywhere.
Underneath all ninety days is Rich · Fit · Sick. Rich is the work, the learning, a rich life. Fit is train every day. Sick is mindset, reading, style and the standard you hold.
The order matters. You can't build a machine with no money coming in, and you can't step out of something that isn't a machine yet.
lessons.story: This is the same path I walked my brother through, from wanting a company to running one fully remote at six figures a month. [STORY: one moment from that journey that shows the three moves in action]
lessons.action: Write the three moves on one page. Next to each, write one sentence on what it would change in your business right now.

lessons.title: Your first seven days
lessons.big_idea: Your first week is a checklist, not a mood. Run it and you start the program with momentum.
talking_points: Day one, finish Course 00. It takes less than an hour.
Day two, post your stage, your target and your date in the community.
Day three, start Course 01 and write your daily standard: train, read, one deep work block, one sales action.
Days four to six, hold the standard every day. If you have no business yet, start Course 02. If you do, start Course 03.
Before the live call, write your one real question, with your numbers attached.
Day seven, post your wins and your misses. Both count.
lessons.story: [STORY: what your own first week looked like when you started your first company]
lessons.action: Copy the seven-day checklist into your calendar today, one item per day, and tick each one off as you go.

courses.assignment_walkthrough: Post three lines in the community: your stage, your monthly target and your date. Be honest about the stage. Most people are one behind where they think. A good post reads like 'Stage 1. $15K a month by March 31.' Add one line on the life it pays for and one line on the problem you're stuck on, so the room can actually help you.

courses.title: The Standard
courses.intro: This course is about you. A business never outgrows the standard of the person running it. We name the beliefs that have been capping you, and you write a daily standard you hold for fourteen days.

lessons.title: You are not the product. The standard is.
lessons.big_idea: If you are the product, the business can't grow past your hours. When the standard is the product, other people can deliver it, and that's what lets you step out.
talking_points: Most service owners think clients are buying them. They're buying a result, delivered to a standard.
If the result only happens when you do it, you own a job. If it happens because there's a standard, you own a business.
Write down what good looks like for your work. Specifically. Turnaround time, quality, how the client is spoken to.
A standard someone else can read and hit is a standard you can hire for, train to and check against.
You can't train someone to be you. You can train them to a standard.
Raise your own standard first. Your team will never hold a higher one than you do.
lessons.story: [STORY: the moment you realized clients were paying for the standard, not for you personally]
lessons.action: Write one paragraph that defines good for your core service, covering quality, speed and communication, clear enough that someone else could check work against it.

lessons.title: The ceiling you installed yourself
lessons.big_idea: Most of what caps your income is a belief you picked up somewhere and never checked. Name it and you can replace it.
talking_points: Every business has a ceiling. Usually the owner put it there.
Listen for the sentences. 'Nobody in my market pays that.' 'If I don't do it myself, it won't be right.' 'I'm not a salesperson.' Those are ceilings.
For each one, ask two questions. Where did I learn this? What's the evidence it's true today?
I charge ten times the market. That's only possible once you stop treating the market rate as a ceiling.
Replace each belief with a sentence you can act on, and one action that tests it this week.
You won't feel ready first. You act, and the belief follows the evidence.
lessons.story: [STORY: a belief that capped you early on, and what broke it]
lessons.action: Write your top three limiting beliefs about money, selling or letting go of the work. Next to each, write one action this week that tests it.

lessons.title: Rich · Fit · Sick
lessons.big_idea: Rich, Fit and Sick run underneath all ninety days. The business and the person get built at the same time.
talking_points: Rich is the work, the learning and a rich life. Not just money in the account.
Fit is train every day. Your energy is the business's energy.
Sick is mindset, reading and style. The standard you hold in how you think, what you learn and how you show up.
Each one gets a daily action. Rich is one deep work block and one sales action. Fit is train. Sick is read.
When one of the three slips, the other two usually follow. Track all three.
This isn't a side project to the business. You're the one running the business, so it is the business.
lessons.story: [STORY: why you named it Rich · Fit · Sick, and what each one looks like in your own week]
lessons.action: Write one daily action for Rich, one for Fit and one for Sick, and do all three tomorrow.

lessons.title: Freedom is the spec, not the prize
lessons.big_idea: Time, location and financial freedom are design requirements. Build them in from day one, or you'll build a business that traps you.
talking_points: Most people build the business first and hope freedom shows up at the end. It doesn't.
Treat freedom like a spec. Before every decision, ask one question: does this make me more needed, or less?
Time freedom means the work doesn't need your hours. Build every service so someone else can deliver it.
Location freedom means nothing needs you in the room. Pick tools, processes and clients that work remote.
Financial freedom means margin and recurring revenue, not one big month. Contracts over one-off jobs.
The finish line is a business you can leave, sell, or run from your phone on the other side of the world, and it holds.
lessons.story: I walked my brother from wanting a company to running one fully remote at six figures a month. [STORY: the early decisions that made running it remote possible]
lessons.action: List your last five business decisions and mark each one 'more needed' or 'less needed'. Reverse one of the 'more needed' ones this week.

lessons.title: Breaking feast or famine
lessons.big_idea: Feast or famine is a loop: chase a job, do it all, get paid, burn out, start again. You break it by selling every day and moving clients onto recurring work.
talking_points: Here's the loop. Chase a job, do it all, get paid, burn out, start again.
It happens because when you're busy delivering, you stop selling. Then the work ends and the pipeline is empty.
Fix one is a sales action every single day, busy or not. That's why it's in your daily standard.
Fix two is recurring revenue. Every client should be on a contract. We cover how in Course 03.
Fix three is getting out of delivery, so delivery can't starve sales. That's The Machine.
Our clients stay 12, 24, 38 months. That's what the other side of feast or famine looks like.
lessons.story: [STORY: your own worst famine month, and what you changed after it]
lessons.action: Write down your revenue for each of the last six months and circle the dips. Next to each dip, write what you stopped doing the month before.

lessons.title: Discipline over motivation
lessons.big_idea: Motivation shows up when it wants. Discipline is a routine you run anyway. Build the routine, then hold the standard.
talking_points: Motivation is a feeling. You can't schedule a feeling. You can schedule a routine.
The Marine Corps taught me about showing up. You don't decide each morning whether you're going. It's already decided.
Make the decisions once. What time you train, when you read, when your deep work block is, when you do your sales action. Then stop renegotiating.
Start smaller than your ego wants. A standard you hold for fourteen days beats a big one you drop on day three.
Track it every day. Tick or no tick. The tracker tells the truth when your mood doesn't.
Miss a day, don't miss two. Get straight back on.
lessons.story: [STORY: a specific moment in the Marine Corps that taught you what showing up means]
lessons.action: Put your four daily actions in your calendar at fixed times for the next fourteen days.

lessons.title: Walkthrough: my day, my week
lessons.big_idea: This is how I actually run my time, the structure behind the standard. Take the structure, not my exact times.
talking_points: I'm going to show you my real calendar. Not the ideal version. The real one.
The fixed blocks go in first: training, reading, deep work. Nothing gets booked over them. [WALKTHROUGH: show your daily fixed blocks and when they happen]
Then the weekly rhythm: team meetings, the scoreboard, sales time. [WALKTHROUGH: show your week and which day holds which meeting]
Everything else fits around those blocks. If something doesn't fit, it gets handed off or it doesn't happen.
Look at what's missing from my calendar as much as what's on it. That's the work I no longer touch. [WALKTHROUGH: name the work you've handed off]
Copy the structure. Your times and your blocks will be different, and that's fine.
lessons.story: [STORY: what your calendar looked like back when everything ran through you]
lessons.action: Build your ideal week in your calendar: fixed blocks first, weekly meetings second, everything else after.

courses.assignment_walkthrough: Write your daily standard as four lines, each with a time and a minimum: train, read, one deep work block, one sales action. For example: 'Train at 6am, 30 minutes minimum. Read 10 pages. Deep work 9 to 11, phone off. One sales action before noon.' Track it every day for fourteen days in the Daily Standard tracker. Good is fourteen out of fourteen. Honest is posting your tally in the community on day fourteen, misses included.

courses.title: Start From Zero
courses.intro: This course is for you if you have no business yet. We're building an online service business, the fastest way I know to go from nothing to cash coming in. By the end you have a service picked, a first offer written and ten conversations booked.

lessons.title: Why a service business
lessons.big_idea: A service business is the fastest way from zero to cash. No inventory, no product to build, and people already pay for it.
talking_points: You don't need a product, an app or an investor. You need something people already pay for and a way to deliver it.
Service businesses get paid up front or on delivery. Cash comes in from your first client.
You can start it from a laptop and run it from anywhere. That's location freedom from day one.
It's the model I've built my own companies on.
The catch: if you do all the work yourself, you've built a job. So from day one, we build it so someone else can deliver.
Recurring service clients are the most valuable thing a small business can have. Our clients stay 12, 24, 38 months.
lessons.story: [STORY: why you started with a service business instead of a product]
lessons.action: Write down three services you've personally paid someone for in the last year, and what you paid for each.

lessons.title: Service business arbitrage
lessons.big_idea: You sell the outcome at a value price and pay a skilled person the market rate to deliver it. The gap is your margin.
talking_points: Arbitrage is simple. The client pays for the result. You pay a skilled person the market rate to do the work. You keep the difference.
Your job is the parts most people can't do: find the client, sell the outcome and hold the standard.
Charge on value, pay the market rate. That's the margin rule we come back to in Course 11.
This isn't cutting corners. The client gets a better result because someone is managing it to a standard.
Know your gap before you sell. If there's no room between what you charge and what the work costs, pick a different service or a higher price.
I charge ten times the market. You get there by selling the result, not the hours.
lessons.story: [STORY: the first job you sold where someone else did the work]
lessons.action: For one service you're considering, write three numbers: the price a client would pay, the cost to have someone else deliver it, and the gap.

lessons.title: Pick your service
lessons.big_idea: Pick something people already pay for, that you can sell, and that someone else can do. It has to pass all three, or you keep looking.
talking_points: Test one: do people already pay for it? Search for it. If you can find businesses selling it and clients buying it, the market is there.
Test two: can you sell it? You should understand the buyer and be able to explain the result in one sentence.
Test three: can someone else do it? If the only person on earth who can deliver it is you, it fails.
Extra points if it's recurring, something clients need every month, not once.
Don't pick on passion. Pick on demand. You can learn to love a business that pays.
Pick one. Not three. You can add offers later. That's Course 13.
lessons.story: [STORY: how you picked your first service, and what you'd tell yourself now]
lessons.action: Score five service ideas against the three tests, using the Service picker worksheet once it's in the Vault, and circle the one that passes all three.

lessons.title: Set it up in a weekend
lessons.big_idea: You need four things to open: a name, a one-page offer, a payment link and a simple CRM. Do it in a weekend and stop there.
talking_points: A name. Clear beats clever. Check the domain and the social handle are free, then move on.
A one-page offer: who it's for, the result, what's included, the price and how to start.
A payment link. If someone says yes on a call, you take the money on the call. Not 'I'll send an invoice later.'
A simple CRM. One place for every lead and every conversation: name, stage, next step, date. A spreadsheet is fine to start.
That's it. No agonizing over a logo, no big website, no business cards. None of those book a conversation.
By Monday morning you should be able to send someone your offer and take payment.
lessons.story: [STORY: what you spent too long on when you set up your first company]
lessons.action: By Sunday night, have your name, your one-page offer, your payment link and your CRM done.

lessons.title: Your first client
lessons.big_idea: Your first client is almost always someone you already know, or someone they know. Start there, and say it plainly.
talking_points: Write a list of everyone you know. Phone contacts, followers, old colleagues, family, friends. Aim for a hundred names.
Mark who could buy it, and who knows someone who could.
Send a plain message: 'I've started a [service] business helping [who] get [result]. Is that something you need, or do you know someone who does?'
Don't pitch in the message. The goal is a conversation, not a sale over text.
On the call, ask about their problem first. Then say the offer, say the number, and stop talking.
Your first client gets your best work. When you deliver, ask for a testimonial and a referral.
lessons.story: [STORY: who your first client was and how that first conversation went]
lessons.action: Build a list of a hundred people you know, send the message to thirty of them, and book every reply into a call.

lessons.title: Your first delivery
lessons.big_idea: You don't have to do the work. You have to find the person who does it, manage the job and keep the client.
talking_points: Find the person before you need them. Line up two or three people who can do the work, and look at their past work.
Run a small paid trial first. Test the work before you commit.
Write down what good looks like: the deliverable, the deadline, the standard. Send it to them in writing.
Put a date on every step, and update the client before they ask.
Check the work before the client sees it. You own the quality, even if you didn't do it.
The goal of the first delivery isn't just to deliver. It's to keep the client and turn them into your next one.
lessons.story: [STORY: a first delivery that went sideways, and what it taught you about managing the work]
lessons.action: Find three people who could deliver your service, review their past work, and message each one for their rate and availability.

lessons.title: Mistakes that kill it in month one
lessons.big_idea: Most new service businesses die of the same few mistakes. Know them in advance and you skip them.
talking_points: Mistake one is building instead of selling. Weeks on a logo and a website, zero conversations. Conversations come first.
Mistake two is picking three services. One service, one buyer, one offer.
Mistake three is pricing low to get the first yes. Low prices bring the wrong clients and leave no room to pay someone else. Price on the result.
Mistake four is doing all the delivery yourself. You stop selling and you're back in feast or famine. Line up your delivery person before you close.
Mistake five is stopping outreach once you land a client. One sales action every day, busy or not.
Mistake six is no follow-up. Most deals close after the fifth touch. Most people stop at one.
lessons.story: [STORY: a month-one mistake you made yourself, or watched someone make]
lessons.action: Go down the list, mark every mistake you're already making, and put the fix for each one in your calendar this week.

courses.assignment_walkthrough: Pick one service, the one that passes all three tests, and put it at the top of your one-page offer. Then book ten conversations this week. Not ten messages sent: ten calls on the calendar with people who could buy or refer. Start with the people you already know and log every one in your CRM with a next step and a date. Good looks like ten names, ten times booked, and a Friday post in the community saying how many turned into proposals.

courses.title: The Offer & Pricing
courses.intro: This week is about what you sell and what you charge for it. Most people have a skill. Very few have an offer. By the end of the week you'll have one sentence anyone understands, three packages, and a price you can say without flinching.

lessons.title: Sell the outcome, not the task
lessons.big_idea: Nobody buys the task. They buy what happens after it. Sell that.
talking_points: Your client doesn't want the task. They want the result the task gets them.
A realtor doesn't want photos. They want the listing sold, faster and for more.
When you sell the task, you get compared on price. When you sell the outcome, you get compared on results.
Here's the test. If your offer describes what you do, rewrite it so it describes what they get.
Ask your best clients why they hired you and write down their exact words. That's your outcome.
The task is the how. Keep it in the back. Lead with the what.
lessons.story: [STORY: a client who hired you for the task but stayed for the outcome, and what they actually cared about]
lessons.action: List every service you sell. Next to each one, write the outcome the client actually pays for, in their words, not yours.

lessons.title: The offer formula
lessons.big_idea: A good offer is one sentence: who it's for, what they get, how fast, and what they don't have to worry about.
talking_points: Here's the formula. I help [who] get [outcome] in [timeframe] without [the thing they're afraid of].
Who means one type of buyer. 'Small businesses' is not a who. Property managers in one city is a who.
The outcome has to be something they can see or count. More leads. More leases. More booked calls.
The timeframe makes it real. Without one, it's a wish.
If someone can't repeat it back after hearing it once, it's too complicated.
Write ten versions and read them out loud. Keep the one that sounds like you talking, not like a website.
lessons.action: Write ten versions of your offer sentence using the formula, read each one out loud, and pick the one you'd say on a call.

lessons.title: Package it
lessons.big_idea: Three ways to sell the same skill. The project gets you in the door, the package makes it easy to buy, and the retainer builds the business.
talking_points: A project is one job, one price, one delivery. Good for a first yes. Bad as a business model.
A package bundles the work into a set result at a set price. The buyer doesn't build the order. You do.
A retainer is the same result every month, on a contract. That's where the business is.
Give them three options. Most people pick the middle, so build the middle to be the one you want them to buy.
Every package has a name, what's in, what's out, a timeline and a price. Nothing vague.
Don't build ten packages. Build three. More choice means a slower yes.
lessons.action: Draft three packages: a starter project, a core package and a monthly retainer. Each one gets a name, what's in, what's out, a timeline and a price.

lessons.title: Recurring revenue
lessons.big_idea: One-off clients mean every month starts at zero. Contracts mean every month starts ahead.
talking_points: If every month starts at zero, you don't have a business. You have a hunt.
Recurring revenue is what lets you hire, plan and step out. Nothing else in this program works without it.
Find the part of your work that repeats. Content every month. Leads every month. A clean building every week. Sell that.
Put it on a contract with a minimum term and a clear way to renew.
The easiest retainer to sell is to a client who already bought a project. Ask at delivery, when they're happiest.
Our clients stay 12, 24, 38 months. That doesn't happen by accident. It starts with an offer built to recur.
lessons.story: Our clients stay 12, 24, 38 months. [STORY: how your first one-off client became a monthly client]
lessons.action: Pick your three happiest past or current clients and offer each one a monthly version of the work you already did for them.

lessons.title: Price on value
lessons.big_idea: Price comes from what the outcome is worth to the buyer. Not your hours. Not what everyone else charges.
talking_points: The market rate is what people charge for the task. I don't sell the task. That's how I charge ten times the market.
Work out what the outcome is worth to the client in dollars. An empty unit for a month. A lost listing. A slow season. Price against that number.
If your price is a small slice of what the result is worth, it's an easy yes, even at ten times the market.
Raise your price on new clients first. Don't apologise. Don't explain. Just quote the new number.
Holding it means no discounts to close. If they need it cheaper, take something out of the package. Never cut the price on the same work.
If nobody ever pushes back on your price, you're too cheap.
lessons.story: [STORY: the first time you raised your price: the number before, the number after, and what the client said]
lessons.action: Write down in dollars what your outcome is worth to one real client. Set your core package price against that number and quote it on your next call.

lessons.title: Guarantees and risk reversal
lessons.big_idea: People don't say no to you. They say no to the risk. Take it off the table with a guarantee you can actually keep.
talking_points: Every buyer is asking one question: what if this doesn't work? Answer it before they ask.
A good guarantee is specific. What you'll deliver, by when, and what happens if you don't.
Guarantee what you control. The work, the deadline, the revisions. Not results that depend on things you don't control.
If you miss, you make it right. Redo it, add a month free, or refund. Pick one and write it down.
Put conditions on it. They show up, they give feedback on time, they use the work. A guarantee is a deal, not a gift.
Done properly, a guarantee costs you almost nothing, because you deliver. If it costs you a lot, the problem is delivery.
lessons.action: Write one guarantee for your core package: what you promise, by when, what you do if you miss, and what the client has to do on their side.

lessons.title: Teardown: a real offer, rebuilt live
lessons.big_idea: Watch an offer go from a list of tasks to one sentence, three packages and a price. Then do the same to yours.
talking_points: Here's the offer as it came in. Notice how much of it is about the person selling, not the person buying.
Line one: who is it for? If I can't tell, we name one buyer.
Line two: what do they get? We swap every task for the outcome it creates.
Then the packages. We cut it to three and make the middle one the obvious pick.
Then the price. We tie it to what the outcome is worth, not to hours.
Last, the risk. We add one guarantee they can't argue with. Then before and after, side by side.
lessons.story: [STORY: pick a real offer to tear down, one of your own early offers or a member's with permission, and strip anything private]
lessons.action: Post your current offer in the community, then post it rebuilt underneath: who, outcome, three packages, price and guarantee.

courses.assignment_walkthrough: Start with the sentence. Use the formula, write ten versions, and read them out loud until one sounds like you talking. Then build three packages under it: a project to get in the door, a core package most people will pick, and a retainer that recurs, each with a name, what's in, what's out, a timeline and a price set on value. Good looks like this: a stranger reads your sentence once and can tell you who it's for and what they get, and you can say every price out loud without flinching.

courses.title: Marketing & Lead Generation
courses.intro: Leads are the engine. When the engine stops, everything else stops with it. This week you build a machine that brings you conversations every week, whether you feel like it or not.

lessons.title: Leads are the whole game
lessons.big_idea: Most problems at this stage are a lead problem in disguise. More real conversations fixes most of it.
talking_points: When there are no leads, every other problem gets louder. You discount. You keep bad clients. You panic.
A lead is a real conversation with someone who could buy. Not a like. Not a follower.
Feast or famine happens because you stop finding work while you're doing work. The fix is to never stop.
Lead generation is a daily job, like training. You don't do it when you feel like it. You just do it.
Know your number: how many conversations it takes to get one client. Then have that many, every week.
If you only fix one thing this month, fix this.
lessons.story: [STORY: a month the leads dried up because you were busy delivering, and what it cost you]
lessons.action: Count how many real sales conversations you had in the last 30 days and write the number down. That's your starting point.

lessons.title: Know exactly who you sell to
lessons.big_idea: You can't find your buyer if you can't describe them. Narrow it until you could list a hundred of them by name.
talking_points: 'Everyone' is not a market. Nobody can find everyone.
Write down the job title, the type of company, the size, the location, and the problem keeping them up at night.
Pick the buyer who has the money and the pain. Not the one who likes you most.
Sell to the person who signs the check. Not the assistant, not the fan.
Go narrow first. You can widen later. Narrow is how you get known.
Here's the test. If you can't list a hundred of them by name, you're either too vague or too narrow.
lessons.action: Write a one-paragraph buyer profile: title, company type, size, location, the problem, and what they already spend money on to fix it.

lessons.title: Build your lists
lessons.big_idea: A list is a name, a company and a way to reach them. Build it before you write a single message.
talking_points: Your buyers already gather somewhere. Directories, associations, LinkedIn, Google Maps, events, hashtags. Go there.
Start with who you already know. Past clients, old colleagues, anyone who's bought from you. That's your warmest list.
Every row needs a name, a company, an email or handle, and a phone number if you can get it.
The list lives in your CRM. Not in your head, not in a notebook.
Add to it every week. A list that stops growing is a business that stops growing.
A hundred real buyers beats ten thousand random names.
lessons.action: Pick your three best sources and get the first 50 names into your CRM today, starting with people you already know.

lessons.title: Outreach that doesn't feel gross
lessons.big_idea: Good outreach is short, about them, and asks for one small thing. Then you follow up until they answer.
talking_points: Outreach feels gross when it's about you. Make it about them and it stops feeling gross.
Four parts. Their name. Something specific you noticed about them. The result you get for people like them. One easy question.
Ask for a reply, not a meeting. 'Worth a quick chat?' is enough.
Use every channel. Email, DMs, a call, LinkedIn. Different people answer in different places.
Plan five touches over two or three weeks before you stop. Most people quit after one.
Put it on the calendar. A set number of messages, every day, in one block, before you open anything else.
lessons.action: Write your first message and four follow-ups, then send the first one to 20 people on your list.

lessons.title: Content that turns into clients
lessons.big_idea: Content that sells shows the result. Before and after, the number, the client saying it. The rest is noise.
talking_points: Nobody hires you because you posted. They hire you because they saw proof.
Proof is the work, the result, and the client saying it. Before and after. The number that moved.
Every post should make your buyer think 'I want that.' If it doesn't, don't post it.
Talk to one buyer, the one from your profile. Not to other people in your industry.
Every piece ends with a next step. Reply, DM, book a call.
Use your best proof everywhere. One result can be ten posts.
lessons.action: Pull three results from client work you've already done and turn each one into a post that ends with a clear next step.

lessons.title: Going viral on purpose
lessons.big_idea: Viral isn't luck. It's a hook, a feeling and a format, and it's only worth it if it points back to your offer.
talking_points: I've gone viral many times. It's not luck. It's a pattern you can repeat.
The first second decides everything. Open with the most surprising thing, not the setup.
People share what makes them feel something. Surprise, awe, a laugh, 'that's so true.'
Study what's already working in your space. Take the format, not the content.
Post a lot. You don't know which one will hit, and volume gives the pattern a chance to work.
Views don't pay. Every viral piece has to point back to your buyer and your offer, or it's just attention.
lessons.story: I've gone viral many times. [STORY: one specific post that went viral: the hook, why it worked, and what it did for the business]
lessons.action: Find five posts that went big in your space, write down the hook and the format of each, and make one of your own using the strongest one.

lessons.title: Referrals and win-backs
lessons.big_idea: The people who already paid you already trust you. Ask them for work and for introductions, on purpose, on a schedule.
talking_points: The cheapest lead you'll ever get is from someone who already paid you.
Ask for referrals at the high point, right after you deliver, when they're happiest.
Make the ask specific. 'Who else do you know who runs a building like this?' beats 'Know anyone?'
Win-backs: go through every client who stopped. Send a short note. What's new, and what you'd do for them now.
Thank every referral. Reward it if it makes sense. People repeat what gets noticed.
Put it on the calendar. Once a month, every past client hears from you.
lessons.action: This week, message every past client, ask your happiest current clients for one specific introduction each, and log every reply in your CRM.

lessons.title: Paid ads
lessons.big_idea: Ads pour fuel on a fire that's already burning. If your offer doesn't sell from outreach yet, ads just lose money faster.
talking_points: Ads don't fix an offer. They make it louder, good or bad.
You're ready when your offer closes from cold outreach, you know your numbers, and you can deliver for more clients.
Know what a client is worth before you spend a dollar. That tells you what you can afford to pay for a lead.
Start small. One audience, one offer, one message. Let it run long enough to learn something.
Send ads to a conversation, not just a page. A call, a form, a DM.
Track every dollar to a lead and every lead to a sale. If you can't track it, don't scale it.
lessons.action: Answer three questions in writing: does my offer close from outreach, what is a client worth, and what can I pay for a lead. If any answer is no or I don't know, don't run ads yet.

lessons.title: The weekly lead scoreboard
lessons.big_idea: Pick one lead number, track it every week, and look at it every Monday. What gets counted gets done.
talking_points: One number: new conversations started this week. That's it.
Every Monday, write last week's number and this week's target, and post it in the community.
Track the inputs too. Messages sent, follow-ups, posts. When the number drops, the inputs tell you why.
Your target comes from the math: conversations it takes to win a client, times the clients you need.
If you miss, don't explain it. Fix the inputs and hit it next week.
This is the number that ends feast or famine. Keep it moving, especially when you're busy.
lessons.action: Set up a one-line scoreboard with your weekly conversation target and post this Monday's number in the community.

courses.assignment_walkthrough: Write your buyer profile first, so every name on the list fits it. Get the 100 into your CRM with a name, a company and a way to reach them, starting with people you already know, then send your first message and follow up until 20 of them write back. A conversation means they replied, not that you sent. Good looks like 100 real buyers in one place, 20 replies logged with a next step, and your first number posted on the Monday scoreboard.

courses.title: Sales
courses.intro: Sales is helping someone make a decision that's good for them. This week you get a call script, an answer to every objection, and a follow-up system that closes. Then you go run ten real calls.

lessons.title: Selling is helping
lessons.big_idea: If your offer really helps, not selling it is the selfish move. Selling is helping the right person decide.
talking_points: If you believe in what you sell, you owe it to the right person to help them buy it.
Pushy is when you care about the sale more than the person. Flip that and the pressure goes away.
Your job on a call is to find out if you can help. If you can't, say so. That builds more trust than any pitch.
Nobody needs your excitement. They need your certainty.
The person who asks the best questions wins the sale.
Sales is a skill. Like training, you get better with reps, not by thinking about it.
lessons.story: [STORY: a sale you almost didn't make because you didn't want to seem pushy, and what that client got from saying yes]
lessons.action: Write down why the right client is better off after buying from you, and read it before every call this week.

lessons.title: The discovery call
lessons.big_idea: The discovery call is where they tell you why they need to buy. Ask, listen, and let them say it themselves.
talking_points: Open by setting the agenda. 'I'll ask a few questions, and if it's a fit I'll show you how we'd work together. Sound good?'
Where are you now? Where do you want to be? What's in the way? That's the core of the call.
Ask what it's costing them to stay where they are, in money and in time.
Ask why now. If nothing's urgent, nothing gets bought.
Find out who decides and what the budget is before you present. Not after.
Talk less than they do. Repeat back what you heard, in their words. Then ask, 'Do you want help fixing that?'
lessons.action: Put your discovery questions on one page in this order: agenda, now, goal, what's in the way, cost, why now, who decides, budget. Use that page on every call.

lessons.title: Present the offer and the price
lessons.big_idea: Tie the offer to what they told you, say the price once, clearly, and then stop talking.
talking_points: Present only what solves the problem they told you about. Use their words back to them.
Walk through the outcome, then how we get there, then the package. In that order.
Say the number once, clearly, with no apology. Then stop talking.
The silence after the price is theirs. Don't fill it. Don't add a discount. Don't explain.
If you have three options, show them and recommend one.
Practise saying your price out loud until it sounds boring to you.
lessons.action: Record yourself presenting your core package and saying the price ten times, until you say the number with no pause and no softener.

lessons.title: Objections
lessons.big_idea: An objection is a question, not a no. Get the real one on the table and answer it.
talking_points: Most objections are a polite way of saying 'I'm not sure yet.' Your job is to find out what they're not sure about.
Price: ask 'Compared to what?' and bring it back to what the problem is costing them.
Timing: ask 'What changes between now and then?' Usually nothing does, and the problem keeps costing them.
“Let me think”: 'Of course. What part do you want to think through? Let's do it now while we're both here.'
“I need to ask my partner”: 'Makes sense. What do you think they'll ask? Let's get them on a call this week.' Better still, ask who else decides on the discovery call.
Write down every objection you hear. The same few come up again and again. Script your answer to each one.
lessons.action: Write your answer to price, timing, “let me think” and “I need to ask my partner”, and say each one out loud before your next call.

lessons.title: Closing
lessons.big_idea: The close is taking the payment while they're still on the call. If they said yes, help them finish.
talking_points: A yes without a payment is a maybe. Take the payment on the call.
Have the payment link and the contract ready before the call starts.
When they say yes: 'Great. I'm sending the link now so we can get you started.' Then stay on while they pay.
Don't celebrate and hang up. Walk them to the next step: the start date, what they need to send, who they'll hear from.
If they can't pay right now, set the exact time it'll happen and put it on the calendar while you're both on.
Ask for the sale. A lot of people run a great call and never ask.
lessons.action: Set up a payment link and a contract for each of your three packages so you can send either one in under a minute on a call.

lessons.title: Follow-up
lessons.big_idea: The money is in the follow-up. Build a system so nobody falls through the cracks.
talking_points: Most deals close after the fifth touch. Most people stop at one. That gap is your edge.
Every call ends with a next step and a date. Never 'I'll follow up.' Say when.
Every lead in your CRM has a stage and a next follow-up date. If it doesn't, it's already lost.
Every touch adds something. A result, a case study, an answer to their question. Not 'just checking in.'
Mix the channels. Email, text, a call, a voice note.
Follow up until you get a yes or a no. A no is fine. Silence is not an answer.
lessons.action: Go through your CRM, give every open lead a stage and a next follow-up date, and send every overdue follow-up today.

lessons.title: High-ticket sales
lessons.big_idea: Bigger deals aren't harder because of the number. They're harder because the risk and the number of people involved go up. Sell to that.
talking_points: As the price goes up, so does the number of people who get a say. One person at the low end. A partner or a boss in the middle. A committee at the top.
The bigger the number, the more the outcome has to be shown in money. Show the math.
Find every person who has a say and talk to each of them. Don't let your champion sell it for you.
Use a proposal. Their problem, the outcome, the plan, the price and the terms, in their words.
High-ticket buyers are buying certainty. Proof, a clear process, a guarantee, and you staying calm.
Expect more touches and a longer cycle. Keep a dated next step on it every single time.
lessons.story: [STORY: your biggest deal: how many people were involved, how long it took, and what finally got it signed]
lessons.action: Take your biggest open opportunity, write down every person who has a say and what each one cares about, and send a proposal using the Vault template.

lessons.title: Drills: real calls, broken down
lessons.big_idea: You get good at sales by reviewing your own calls. Listen back, find where it turned, and fix what you say.
talking_points: Record every call, with permission. You can't fix what you can't hear.
Listen for three moments: when they told you the real problem, when you said the price, and when the objection came.
Check who talked more. If it was you, that's the first fix.
For every miss, write the line you'll say instead. Then say it out loud until it's yours.
We break down real calls here. What worked, what didn't, and what to say instead.
Bring one call to the live call every week. That's how this gets fast.
lessons.story: [STORY: a real recorded call, yours or a member's with permission, broken down: the moment it turned and the line that should have been said]
lessons.action: Record your next call, listen back within 24 hours, and write three things: what worked, what didn't, and what you'll say instead.

courses.assignment_walkthrough: Run all ten calls off the same discovery page and the same presentation, so you're testing the script, not making it up each time. Record each one, and straight after the call log every objection word for word, what you said back, whether it closed, and the dated next step. After ten, group the objections. You'll see the same few repeat, so rewrite your answer to the top ones. Good looks like ten logged calls, a next step on every open deal, and an objection sheet you'll use on every call after this.

courses.title: Delivery & Client Experience
courses.intro: This is week five. Money's coming in, so now we keep it. This course is about getting the work done on a date, at a standard, without you doing it, and keeping clients for years instead of months.

lessons.title: Make every client feel like your only client
lessons.big_idea: Clients don't leave because of the work. They leave because they feel forgotten. Make every one of them feel like the only one, and they stay.
talking_points: Every client is quietly asking one question: do they remember me?
Feeling like the only client isn't about doing more work. It's about attention: names, details, speed.
Write down what each client cares about, their goals, their people, how they like to hear from you, and read it before every touch.
Reply fast. Same business day is the floor. Speed tells them they matter.
The small things carry the most weight. Remember their launch date. Send the result before they ask. Notice their win and say so.
Build this into the system, not your memory. If it lives in your head, it leaves when you step out.
lessons.story: [STORY: a client who stayed because of one small thing you remembered]
lessons.action: For every active client, write one line on what they care about most and how they want to hear from you, and put it in your CRM.

lessons.title: From order to delivered
lessons.big_idea: Every job follows the same path from the moment they pay to the moment it's delivered. Write the path down, put a date on every step, and the work stops depending on you.
talking_points: Start at the moment the money lands. End at the moment the client says got it. Everything in between is your delivery process.
Most of you have never written this down. It lives in your head, and that's why it breaks when you're busy.
List every step in order: payment, onboarding, kickoff, production, review, delivery, follow-up.
Every step gets an owner and a committed date. Not soon. A date.
Give the client the dates up front. A client who knows what's next doesn't chase you.
When a step slips, you see it on the map before the client feels it.
lessons.story: [STORY: a job that went sideways because nobody owned a step]
lessons.action: Write your delivery steps from payment to delivered, with an owner and a number of days next to each one.

lessons.title: Quality control without doing it yourself
lessons.big_idea: The standard can't live in your eye. Put it on a checklist, build in a review, and someone else can hit it every time.
talking_points: If you're the only one who can tell good from bad, you're still the bottleneck.
Write the standard down. Make it specific enough that two different people would grade the same job the same way.
Turn it into a checklist the person doing the work runs before they hand it in.
Add one review by someone other than the person who did the work. Two sets of eyes before the client sees anything.
When something slips through, don't just fix the job. Fix the checklist so it can't happen again.
You check the checklist, not every job. Spot-check a few a week and let the system do the rest.
lessons.story: [STORY: the moment you realized you were checking every job yourself]
lessons.action: Write a ten-line quality checklist for your main deliverable, and run the next job through it before it reaches you.

lessons.title: Communication that keeps clients
lessons.big_idea: Update them before they ask. If a client has to chase you, you've already lost some of their trust.
talking_points: Silence is where clients start to worry. Worry turns into doubt, and doubt turns into churn.
Set a rhythm and tell them what it is: a kickoff message, an update at every step, a recap when it's delivered.
Bad news goes out early, and it comes with a plan. Never let a client find a problem before you tell them.
Keep updates short: what's done, what's next, and when they'll hear from you again.
One channel per client. Scattered messages make the business look scattered.
Template every update so your team sends them, not you.
lessons.story: [STORY: a client who almost left because they didn't hear from you]
lessons.action: Write three message templates, kickoff, progress update and delivered, and use them on every active job this week.

lessons.title: Revisions, complaints and saving a relationship
lessons.big_idea: An upset client handled well becomes your biggest fan. Listen, own it, fix it fast, and follow up after.
talking_points: Set the revision rules before the work starts: how many rounds, what counts as a revision, and what's a new request.
When a complaint comes in, don't defend. Listen all the way through, then say back what you heard.
Own your part plainly. We missed that, and here's what we're doing about it. No excuses.
Fix it faster than they expect. Speed on a problem buys back more trust than the original job earned.
Follow up once it's fixed and ask if it's right now. That call is where fans are made.
Then find the cause and change the process, so the next client never sees it.
lessons.story: [STORY: an upset client who became one of your best]
lessons.action: Write your revision policy in three sentences and add it to your proposal and your onboarding.

lessons.title: Retention and churn
lessons.big_idea: Clients leave for a few predictable reasons. Know them, watch for the signs, and act before the cancellation email.
talking_points: Churn is a hole in the bottom of the bucket. You can't market your way out of it.
Clients leave because they stop seeing results, they feel ignored, something went wrong and wasn't fixed, or they never understood what they were paying for.
Watch the warning signs: slower replies, skipped calls, questions about the contract, a new decision-maker on their side.
Show them the result on a schedule. A monthly recap of what you did and what it produced. Make the value visible.
Hold a review before every renewal. Talk about the next twelve months, not the last invoice.
Track how long each client stays, and write down why the ones who left, left. That list tells you what to fix.
lessons.story: [STORY: the client you lost and what it taught you]
lessons.action: List every client who left in the last year, write the real reason next to each, and fix the most common one this month.

lessons.title: Walkthrough: contracts that run for years
lessons.big_idea: Our clients stay 12, 24, 38 months because the contract, the delivery and the communication are built for the long run from day one.
talking_points: Our clients stay 12, 24, 38 months. That isn't luck. It's built in.
It starts at the sale: a recurring offer, a contract with a term, and clear expectations on what they get every month.
Then delivery on a date, every time, at the standard. Consistency is what they're really paying for.
Then the rhythm: updates before they ask, a monthly recap, and a review before every renewal.
I'm going to walk you through how we set this up, start to finish, so you can copy it.
Read the Recurring Client Playbook and the Grove Central white paper in the Vault alongside this lesson.
lessons.story: Our clients stay 12, 24, 38 months. [STORY: walk through one long-term client: how they came in, what kept them, and where they are now]
lessons.action: Write down why your longest client has stayed, then build those reasons into your contract and onboarding for every new client.

courses.assignment_walkthrough: Start at payment and end at delivered. Write every step in order, then put an owner and a committed date on each one, counted in days from kickoff. Good looks like a one-page map anyone on your team could follow, where the client knows every date before the work starts. If a step has no date, the assignment isn't done.

courses.title: Buy Back Your Time
courses.intro: Week six. You can't build a business that runs without you while every hour goes into doing the work. This week we find out where your time actually goes, decide what only you should be doing, and hand off the first thing.

lessons.title: What your hour is worth
lessons.big_idea: Know what your hour is worth. Anything you can pay someone less than that to do well, you should stop doing.
talking_points: Take what you want to earn in a year and divide it by the hours you want to work. That's your hour.
Now look at your day. How much of it goes to work worth a fraction of that number?
Every hour on low-value work is an hour not spent selling, building the team, or living your life.
Doing it yourself to save money is expensive. It costs you the money you'd make with that hour.
Write your number down. You'll use it to decide every handoff from here.
lessons.story: [STORY: when you realized you were doing work worth far less than your time]
lessons.action: Calculate your hourly number from your target and write it at the top of your time audit.

lessons.title: The time audit
lessons.big_idea: You can't buy back time you haven't measured. Track one full week, honestly, in thirty-minute blocks.
talking_points: For one week, write down what you do in thirty-minute blocks. All of it. Email, calls, edits, scrolling.
Write it as you go, not at the end of the day. Memory lies.
Tag each block: does it make money, does it run the business, or does it just keep you busy?
Then mark the value. Is this worth your hourly number, or could someone else do it for far less?
At the end of the week, add it up. Most people are shocked by how little time goes to the work only they can do.
lessons.story: [STORY: what your own first time audit showed you]
lessons.action: Start your time audit today: thirty-minute blocks for seven days, every block tagged.

lessons.title: The only things you should be doing
lessons.big_idea: Only a short list of things belongs on your plate. Everything else is a candidate to hand off.
talking_points: At this stage your job is short: selling, setting the standard, hiring the right people, and deciding where the company goes.
Everything else is a candidate to hand off. Not someday. Now.
Sort your audit into four groups: only you can do it, someone could do it with training, someone could do it today, and nobody should be doing it.
Kill the last group first. Then hand off what someone could do today.
If you love doing the work, keep it as a choice, not a requirement. The business can't depend on it.
lessons.action: Write the list of the only things you should be doing, five items at most, and pin it where you work.

lessons.title: Your first handoff
lessons.big_idea: Hand off the repeatable task that gives you back the most hours. One task handed off properly beats ten half-delegated.
talking_points: Look at your audit and find the task that repeats and eats the most hours. That's your first handoff.
Record yourself doing it once, screen and voice. That recording is the first draft of the training.
Write what done looks like and when it's due. Outcome, standard, deadline.
Have them do it while you check. Then have them do it without you.
It will be worse at first. That's the price. Correct it, update the checklist, and don't take it back.
Count the hours you get back every week. That number is your proof.
lessons.story: [STORY: the first thing you ever handed off, and how it went]
lessons.action: Pick your biggest repeatable task, record yourself doing it once, and hand it to someone by the end of the week.

lessons.title: Tools and AI that buy back hours this week
lessons.big_idea: Before you hire, automate. The fastest hours you'll get back come from tools you can set up this week.
talking_points: Not every handoff needs a person. Some need a tool.
Start with scheduling. A booking link instead of back-and-forth emails.
Then payments. A payment link and automatic invoices instead of chasing money.
Use AI for first drafts: proposals, emails, captions, recaps. You edit. You never start from blank.
Make a template for every message you send more than twice.
Never automate the relationship. Tools take the admin. Keep the human where it counts.
lessons.action: Pick three repeated admin tasks from your audit and set up a tool, template or AI prompt for each one this week.

lessons.title: Protect the time you win back
lessons.big_idea: Time you win back fills right back up unless you decide in advance where it goes.
talking_points: Hours you free up don't stay free. They fill with something worse unless you protect them.
Decide what the time is for before you win it back: selling, hiring, training, or your life.
Put it on the calendar as a block and treat it like a client meeting.
Watch for work creeping back. If a task you handed off lands on your desk again, hand it back.
Say no more. Every yes to something small is a no to something that matters.
Run the time audit again every quarter. It drifts.
lessons.story: [STORY: what you do with the hours you've won back, and how you guard them]
lessons.action: Block the hours you've won back on your calendar for the next four weeks, and write what each block is for.

courses.assignment_walkthrough: Track every thirty-minute block for seven days, as you go, and tag each one by value. At the end of the week, rank the tasks by hours spent and how often they repeat. The top one is your handoff. Good looks like a full week with no gaps, a clear number of hours you'll get back, and that task handed off with a recording and a definition of done before next week's call.

courses.title: Recruiting & Hiring
courses.intro: Week seven. Talent is the business. You can have the best offer and the best systems and still be stuck if the wrong people are doing the work. This week you build a hiring process that finds good people on demand, so nobody, including you, is irreplaceable.

lessons.title: Talent is the business
lessons.big_idea: Your business will never be better than the people doing the work. Hiring isn't a side task. It is the job.
talking_points: Your business is only as good as the people doing the work.
I built my own companies and trained the people who now run them. That's the only reason I can step away.
Hiring isn't something you do when you're desperate. It's a process you run all the time.
The right person makes you money. The wrong person costs you clients, time and reputation.
Your job is to find people better than you at the work and give them a standard to hit.
lessons.story: I built my own companies and trained the people who now run them. [STORY: your first great hire and what changed after]
lessons.action: List every role in your business today and who does it, then circle every role where the answer is you.

lessons.title: Contractors or employees
lessons.big_idea: Start with contractors for the work. Move to employees when a role is full-time, core to the business, and needs you directing how it's done.
talking_points: Contractors are paid for the output. Employees are paid for their time, and you direct how they work.
Early on, contractors make sense. You pay per job, scale up and down, and test before you commit.
Move to an employee when the role is full-time, core to the business, and you need to direct how and when the work gets done.
The rules on who counts as a contractor are different in every country and state. Get it checked by an accountant or attorney. Don't guess.
Whichever you choose, the standard is the same. Same checklist, same deadlines, same expectations.
lessons.action: For each role you'll fill in the next 90 days, write contractor or employee and why, then confirm it with your accountant.

lessons.title: Where to find good people
lessons.big_idea: Good people are anywhere in the world. Go where they already show their work.
talking_points: If the work can be done remotely, you're not limited to your city. The whole world is your pool.
Look where people show their work: portfolios, industry communities, freelance platforms and social.
Referrals from people you trust are the fastest filter. Ask your best people who they'd hire.
Post the role where your kind of person already spends time, not just on a job board.
Always be looking. The best time to find someone is before you need them.
lessons.action: Pick three places your ideal hire already shows their work, and save ten candidates from them this week.

lessons.title: The post, the screen, the paid trial
lessons.big_idea: Test the work before you commit. A clear post, a fast screen and a paid trial tell you more than any interview.
talking_points: The post says what the role is, what done looks like, what it pays, and how to apply. Put one specific instruction in it so you can see who actually reads.
The screen is a short call or a few written questions. You're checking communication, reliability and fit. Not charm.
The paid trial is a real piece of work, with a deadline and your checklist. Same as the actual job.
Always pay for the trial. It's fair, and it brings out the serious people.
Watch everything. Did they hit the deadline, ask good questions, follow the standard? That's how they'll work for you.
lessons.action: Write your job post with one instruction buried in it, and design a paid trial that matches the real job.

lessons.title: Score and choose
lessons.big_idea: Hire slow, let go fast. Score every candidate on the same criteria and decide on evidence, not on feeling.
talking_points: Hire slow, let go fast.
Build a simple scorecard before you see a single candidate: quality of work, hit the deadline, communication, followed the standard, attitude.
Score every trial the same way, one to five, with a sentence of evidence next to every score.
Choose on the numbers. If you're talking yourself into someone, the answer is no.
Start every hire on a trial period with clear targets. If they miss and don't improve, let them go fast. Waiting only makes it worse.
lessons.story: [STORY: a hire you made on gut feeling and what it cost you]
lessons.action: Build a five-line scorecard and score every paid trial on it before you choose.

lessons.title: Onboarding and protecting your business
lessons.big_idea: A good first week makes a good hire stick. The paperwork and the access rules protect you if it doesn't.
talking_points: Before anyone starts: a signed agreement, an NDA, and clear terms on who owns the work.
Have an attorney look at your agreements once. Then use them every single time.
Give access only to what they need. Their own logins, never yours. Shared passwords are a risk.
Their first week: your SOPs, your checklist, one small real job, and a check-in at the end of it.
Keep a list of everything each person has access to, so you can shut it off in one afternoon if you need to.
lessons.action: Put together your onboarding pack, agreement, NDA, access list and first-week plan, before your next hire starts.

lessons.title: Keep a bench
lessons.big_idea: Five good people ready for every role, at all times. Nobody is irreplaceable, including you.
talking_points: Five good people ready for every role, at all times.
Everyone who did well on a trial but didn't get the role goes on the bench. Stay in touch.
Give bench people small paid jobs now and then, so they know your standard and you know they're still good.
When someone leaves or work spikes, you call the bench. No panic, no scramble.
A bench keeps the standard high. When nobody is irreplaceable, nobody gets to coast.
lessons.story: [STORY: a time someone left and you had nobody ready]
lessons.action: Start a bench list for your most important role and get it to five names.

courses.assignment_walkthrough: Write one post for the role you need most, with the pay, what done looks like, and one instruction that tests who reads. Run three paid trials on the same real task, with the same deadline and the same checklist. Score all three on your scorecard and write the evidence down. Good looks like a hire you'd choose on the numbers alone, and two strong runners-up who go straight onto your bench.

courses.title: Delegation & Systems
courses.intro: This week we take everything out of your head and put it where other people can use it. If the business only works when you remember things, you don't have a business, you have a memory. By Friday you'll have your three most repeated jobs written down so someone else can run them.

lessons.title: If it's in your head, it isn't a system
lessons.big_idea: Anything that only works because you remember it will break the day you stop remembering. A system is something another person can run, the same way, without asking you.
talking_points: Every time someone asks you how to do something, that's proof it isn't written down.
Your memory is the most expensive storage in the company, because it only works when you're awake and in the room.
A system has three parts: the steps, the standard for done, and where it lives so anyone can find it.
You don't need to systemize everything. Start with the work you repeat every week.
The test is simple. Could someone new do this job tomorrow, from the document alone, and get it right? If not, it isn't a system yet.
lessons.story: [STORY: a time something broke because it only lived in your head]
lessons.action: For the next three days, write down every question anyone asks you about how something is done. That list is your first set of SOPs.

lessons.title: Write an SOP in 30 minutes
lessons.big_idea: An SOP doesn't need to be perfect. It needs to exist, be short, and get better every time someone uses it.
talking_points: Don't write it from a blank page. Record yourself doing the job once, screen and voice, then turn the recording into steps.
Every SOP has the same shape: what this is for, when it happens, who owns it, the steps, and what done looks like.
Write each step as one action. Start it with a verb. If a step has an 'and' in it, it's two steps.
Put the standard in writing. 'Edit the video' is not a standard. 'Under 60 seconds, captions on, logo in the last frame' is.
Hand it to the person who'll do the job and let them run it while you watch. Every place they get stuck, fix the document, not the person.
Set a timer for 30 minutes. When it goes off, the SOP is done. Version two comes from real use.
lessons.action: Pick one job you do every week. Record yourself doing it, then write the SOP from the recording in 30 minutes using the SOP template.

lessons.title: The CRM
lessons.big_idea: One place for every lead, client, job and dollar. If it isn't in the CRM, it didn't happen.
talking_points: A CRM is not a contact list. It's the place the whole company runs from.
At minimum you need four things in it: people, deals, jobs and money. Leads come in, become deals, become jobs, become paid invoices.
Every deal has a stage. Every job has an owner and a date. Every invoice has a status. That's how you see the business without asking anyone.
Pick one tool and move everything into it. Two systems means nobody trusts either one.
The rule for the team is simple: if it isn't in the CRM, it didn't happen.
Start simple. You can add fields later. You can't fix a CRM nobody uses.
lessons.story: [SHOW: screen-share the CRM we run on, from a new lead to a paid invoice]
lessons.action: Set up your CRM with four tables or sections: people, deals, jobs and money. Move every open lead and every active client into it this week.

lessons.title: Delegate so it sticks
lessons.big_idea: Outcome, standard, deadline, check-in. Miss one of the four and the work comes back to you.
talking_points: Most delegation fails because the owner hands off a task, not an outcome. Tell them what the finished result is, not just what to do.
Then give them the standard. Show them what good looks like. Point to the SOP or an example.
Then the deadline. A date and a time, not 'when you get a chance'.
Then the check-in. Agree when you'll look at it before it's due, so problems show up early, not on the deadline.
When the work comes back wrong, don't take it back and do it yourself. Show them the gap against the standard and let them fix it.
If you redo their work, you've just taught them that you'll always redo their work.
lessons.story: [STORY: a handoff that came back to you, and which of the four was missing]
lessons.action: Delegate one task this week using all four: write the outcome, the standard, the deadline and the check-in time in one message, and send it.

lessons.title: The machine
lessons.big_idea: People, process, tools and AI, working together. Each one does the job it's best at, and none of them depend on you.
talking_points: People do the work that needs judgement, taste and relationships.
Process tells the people exactly how it's done, so the result is the same no matter who does it.
Tools hold the information and move it along: the CRM, the calendar, the payment link, the shared drive.
AI takes the repeatable writing, sorting and first drafts, so your people spend their time on what matters.
When something breaks, ask which of the four failed. Most of the time it isn't the person, it's a missing process.
Your job is to build and tune the machine, not to be a part inside it.
lessons.action: Take one service you sell and map it on one page: who does each step, which SOP covers it, which tool it lives in, and where AI can do the first draft.

lessons.title: Walkthrough: the operating system behind my agency
lessons.big_idea: How a national company runs without me in the room. It's not talent or luck. It's the same SOPs, CRM and rhythm you're building this week.
talking_points: I'm going to show you the actual operating system, not a diagram of it.
Watch how a lead comes in, gets worked, becomes a client, gets delivered and gets paid, and notice where I'm not involved.
Every job has an owner, a date and a standard. That's why nobody needs to call me.
The team doesn't ask me how to do things. They check the SOP, and if the SOP is wrong, they fix it.
None of this was built in one go. It was built one SOP and one handoff at a time.
lessons.story: A national agency runs without me in the room. [SHOW: walk through the operating system end to end, from lead to paid] [STORY: the first time you saw it run without you]
lessons.action: Compare your business to the walkthrough. Write down the three places where work still stops and waits for you. Those are your next three SOPs.

courses.assignment_walkthrough: Pick your three most repeated jobs, the ones you or your team do every single week. Record yourself doing each one once, then write each SOP in 30 minutes: purpose, owner, trigger, steps, and what done looks like. Hand each SOP to the person who'll run it and fix the document every time they get stuck. Good looks like someone else completing all three jobs this week, from the document alone, without asking you a single question.

courses.title: Leadership & Managing a Team
courses.intro: You've got people now. This week is about leading them, not doing their job for them. We'll set the standard, build a weekly rhythm, and get you ready to hand the keys to your first manager.

lessons.title: From doer to leader
lessons.big_idea: Your job is no longer to do the work. Your job is to make sure the work gets done to the standard, without you.
talking_points: The skills that got you here, doing the work fast and well, are now what's holding the business back.
Every time you jump in and do it yourself, you take the rep away from your team.
A leader's output is the team's output. Measure yourself by what they ship, not what you ship.
This feels slower at first. It is slower at first. Then it's the only way to get faster.
Your new work is setting the standard, hiring, training, removing roadblocks and keeping score.
lessons.story: [STORY: the moment you realized doing the work yourself was the bottleneck]
lessons.action: List everything you did last week. Mark each item 'doer' or 'leader'. Pick one doer item and hand it off this week.

lessons.title: Set the standard, and hold it
lessons.big_idea: The standard is whatever you tolerate. Write it down, show it, and hold it every single time.
talking_points: If it isn't written, it isn't a standard. It's a mood.
Show people what good looks like with real examples, not adjectives.
You set the standard by what you let slide. Let it slide once and that's the new standard.
Hold it the same way for everyone, every time. Consistency is what makes people trust it.
Hold yourself to it first. The team watches what you do, not what you say. That's what the Marine Corps taught me about showing up.
When the standard is clear, you don't have to be the bad guy. The standard does the talking.
lessons.story: [STORY: a time you let the standard slip, and what it cost]
lessons.action: Write the standard for your core deliverable in one page with two examples of good and one of not good enough. Share it with the team.

lessons.title: The weekly rhythm
lessons.big_idea: Meetings, scoreboards and check-ins. One weekly meeting and one scoreboard will fix most of your team problems.
talking_points: A team without a rhythm runs on interruptions. A team with a rhythm runs on a calendar.
One weekly team meeting, same day, same time, same agenda. Keep it short.
The agenda: the scoreboard, wins, what's stuck, and who owns what by when.
The scoreboard is three to five numbers that tell you if the week went well. Leads, sales, jobs delivered on time, cash collected.
Short one-on-ones with each direct report catch problems before they turn into fires.
If something can wait for the weekly meeting, it waits for the weekly meeting.
lessons.action: Book your weekly team meeting as a recurring event and pick the three to five numbers that go on your scoreboard.

lessons.title: Accountability without micromanaging
lessons.big_idea: Trust, with a scoreboard. You don't watch people work. You watch the numbers and the standard.
talking_points: Micromanaging is what happens when you don't have a scoreboard.
Give people ownership of an outcome and a number, then leave them alone to hit it.
Every task has one owner and one date. Two owners means no owner.
When a number is off, ask questions first. What happened, what's the plan, what do you need from me.
Follow up on every commitment. If you don't check, people learn it doesn't matter.
Trust is earned by hitting the numbers. Give more room to the people who keep hitting them.
lessons.action: Give each person on your team one number they own and put it on the scoreboard with their name next to it.

lessons.title: Hard conversations
lessons.big_idea: Feedback, letting people go, and doing it well. The conversation you're avoiding is costing you more than the conversation itself.
talking_points: Give feedback early, in private, and about the work, not the person.
Be specific. Say what happened, what the standard is, and what needs to change by when.
Don't stack up problems and unload them all at once. Small and often beats big and late.
Hire slow, let go fast. If you've given clear feedback and it isn't changing, it's time.
When you let someone go, be direct, be kind, and be brief. Thank them, keep their dignity intact, and cut access the same day.
Everyone else on the team already knows who isn't pulling their weight. They're waiting to see if you do.
lessons.story: [STORY: a hard conversation you put off too long]
lessons.action: Name the one conversation you've been avoiding. Write down what happened, the standard, and what needs to change, then have it this week.

lessons.title: Your first manager
lessons.big_idea: Who, when, and how to hand them the keys. Your first manager is the person who takes the day-to-day off your plate.
talking_points: You need a manager when you're the one answering every question and approving every job.
Look inside first. The best first manager is usually someone who already holds the standard without being told.
Don't promote your best doer just because they're the best doer. Promote the person others already go to.
Hand over in steps. First they run the weekly meeting. Then they own the scoreboard. Then they own hiring and handoffs.
