Give them the authority to make calls, not just the responsibility. And don't overrule them in front of the team.
Your job becomes coaching one person instead of managing everyone.
lessons.story: [STORY: choosing your first manager, and what you'd do differently]
lessons.action: Write down who your first manager is, or will be, and the first thing you'll hand them: running the weekly meeting.

lessons.title: Leading a remote team
lessons.big_idea: Culture when nobody's in the same room. Remote works when everything is written, everything is scheduled, and the standard is visible.
talking_points: Remote teams run on writing. If it isn't in the CRM, the SOP or the chat, it didn't happen.
Keep the rhythm sacred. The weekly meeting matters more when nobody shares an office.
Cameras on for the team meeting. You need to see people, and they need to see you.
Default to async for updates and keep live time for decisions and problems.
Hire people anywhere in the world, and judge them on output, not hours online.
Culture is what you celebrate and what you tolerate. Post the wins publicly and handle the misses privately.
lessons.story: I walked my brother from wanting a company to running one fully remote at six figures a month.
lessons.action: Move all team updates into one written channel and post the scoreboard there every week before the meeting.

courses.assignment_walkthrough: Book one recurring weekly team meeting, same day and time, and put it on everyone's calendar. Build one scoreboard with three to five numbers, each with one owner's name next to it. Run the first meeting with a fixed agenda: scoreboard, wins, what's stuck, and who owns what by when. Good looks like a meeting that ends on time with every open item owned and dated, and a scoreboard the team can read without you explaining it.

courses.title: Money
courses.intro: This week we get honest about the numbers. Most owners don't know their margin, their cash or how many leads it takes to hit their month. By Friday you'll have a target, and the weekly lead number it takes to get there.

lessons.title: Set the target
lessons.big_idea: Pick a monthly revenue number and a date. A target without a date is a wish.
talking_points: Start with the life you want and work out what it costs. That's the floor for your number.
Pick one monthly revenue number. Not a range. One number.
Put a date on it. The month you'll hit it for the first time.
Make it big enough to change how you work, and close enough that you'll still believe it next month.
Write it where you'll see it every day, and post it in the community.
lessons.story: [STORY: the first revenue target you set, and what happened]
lessons.action: Write your monthly revenue target and the date you'll hit it. Post both in the community.

lessons.title: Work it backwards
lessons.big_idea: Every revenue target breaks down into a weekly number of leads and conversations. Do the math once and you'll know exactly what to do every Monday.
talking_points: Start with the target. Divide it by your average client value per month. That's how many clients you need.
Then use your close rate. If you close one in four calls, you need four calls for every client.
Then your show-up and booking rate. How many conversations does it take to book one call?
Then divide by the weeks. That gives you the weekly lead number.
Here's the shape of it: target, divided by client value, times calls per close, times leads per call, divided by weeks. Plug in your own numbers.
If you don't know your close rate yet, use your last ten calls. Real numbers beat guesses.
lessons.action: Fill in the revenue target calculator with your real numbers and write down your weekly lead number.

lessons.title: The numbers every owner knows
lessons.big_idea: Revenue, margin, cash and pipeline. If you can't say these four from memory, you're guessing.
talking_points: Revenue is what you billed this month. Not what you hope to bill.
Margin is what's left after you pay for the work. That's the money that runs the business.
Cash is what's actually in the bank, and what's coming in and going out in the next 30 days.
Pipeline is the open deals and what they're worth. It tells you what next month looks like.
Check all four every week. It takes ten minutes once your CRM and books are set up.
Profit on paper doesn't pay bills. Cash does.
lessons.action: Write down your revenue, margin, cash and pipeline as of today. If you can't find one, that's the first thing to fix.

lessons.title: Margins
lessons.big_idea: Charge on value, pay the market rate. Your margin lives in the gap between the two.
talking_points: Price on what the result is worth to the client, not on your hours or your costs.
Pay the people who do the work a fair market rate for that work.
The gap between the two is your margin, and your margin funds sales, management, growth and your own pay.
If your margin is thin, you have a pricing problem or a delivery problem. Usually pricing.
This is how I charge ten times the market and hold it. The client pays for the outcome, and the delivery cost is set by the market.
Know your margin on every package. If one package doesn't make money, fix it or kill it.
lessons.story: [STORY: the first time you raised your price]
lessons.action: Work out the margin on each of your packages: price minus the cost to deliver it. Flag any package below the margin you need.

lessons.title: Cash, bills and paying yourself
lessons.big_idea: Know what's coming, and when. Cash problems are almost always timing problems you didn't see coming.
talking_points: Keep a simple cash calendar: what's coming in, what's going out, and on what date, for the next 30 days.
Get paid up front or on a schedule. Recurring contracts make cash predictable.
Invoice the day the work is delivered, not when you remember.
Know your fixed bills every month: payroll, contractors, software, rent. No surprises.
Pay yourself on a set amount and a set date. If the business can't pay you, that's information, not a reason to skip it quietly.
Chase overdue invoices every week. Money owed to you is not money you have.
lessons.action: Build a 30-day cash calendar listing every payment in and every bill out, with dates. Set the date and amount you pay yourself.

lessons.title: Organize the money
lessons.big_idea: Accounts, books and peace of mind. Separate accounts, clean books every month, and nobody guesses.
talking_points: Business money and personal money never live in the same account.
Set up separate accounts so you can see at a glance what's for operating, what's for taxes, and what's for profit.
Get the books done every month, not once a year. A bookkeeper is one of the first hires that pays for itself.
Set aside tax money every time you get paid, so tax time isn't a crisis.
Keep every invoice and every receipt in one place your bookkeeper can reach.
Clean books are what let you make decisions fast, and what let you sell the business one day.
lessons.action: Open separate accounts for operating and taxes if you don't have them, and book a monthly close with your bookkeeper.

lessons.title: Hit the number every month
lessons.big_idea: The monthly scoreboard. Check the number every week, so the end of the month is never a surprise.
talking_points: Put the monthly target, the weekly lead number, closed revenue to date and pipeline on one scoreboard.
Look at it every Monday. If you're behind in week two, you still have time to fix it.
When you're behind, go back to the lead number. It's almost always a leads problem.
At the end of the month, write down what you hit, what you missed and why. One line each.
Then set next month's target. Same process, every month.
Hitting the number once is good. Hitting it every month is a business.
lessons.action: Build your monthly scoreboard with target, weekly lead number, revenue closed and pipeline, and review it every Monday this month.

courses.assignment_walkthrough: Start with your monthly target and the date. Then work it backwards with your real numbers: average client value, close rate from your last ten calls, and how many conversations it takes to book one call. Divide down to a weekly lead number and write it next to the target. Good looks like one line you can read every Monday, the target, the date and the number of leads it takes each week, built on real data, not hope.

courses.title: Get Out of the Work
courses.intro: This is the week you start replacing yourself. Not all at once. One role at a time, in a set order, until the business runs from your phone and you're the owner, not the operator.

lessons.title: A finished business has a definition
lessons.big_idea: A finished business is one you can leave, sell, or run from your phone on the other side of the world, and it holds. If it can't do that yet, it isn't finished. It's a job you own.
talking_points: Most owners never finish their business because they never defined what finished means.
Here's the definition: you can leave it, sell it, or run it from your phone anywhere, and revenue, delivery and clients all hold.
Test it honestly. If you disappeared for thirty days, what breaks first? That's what you work on.
Finished doesn't mean you stop working. It means the business doesn't need you to work.
Time freedom, location freedom and financial freedom aren't the reward at the end. They're the spec you build to.
Everything else in this course is just closing the gap between where you are and that definition.
lessons.story: [STORY: the moment you realized one of your businesses was finished — the first time it held without you]
lessons.action: Write the thirty-day test: list what would break in your business if you vanished for thirty days, in the order it would break.

lessons.title: The replacement map
lessons.big_idea: Every hat you wear is a role someone else can hold. The replacement map lists each one, who takes it, and the date you hand it over.
talking_points: Write down every role you play in the business. Not tasks, roles: delivery, sales, hiring, client communication, operations, finance.
Next to each role, write how many hours a week it takes you and what it costs to replace.
Then write who takes it. A name if you have one, a job post if you don't.
Then a date. A role without a handoff date is a wish, not a plan.
The order matters: delivery first, then sales, then management. That's the order I'll teach this week.
When the map has a name and a date next to every role except owner, you have a plan to get out.
lessons.action: Build your replacement map: every role, hours per week, who replaces you, and the handoff date.

lessons.title: Step out of delivery first
lessons.big_idea: The work goes before anything else. Delivery is the easiest role to systemize and the one eating most of your hours.
talking_points: Delivery is first because it's the most repeatable thing you do, and repeatable means it can be written down.
If you're still doing the work, you have no time to sell, hire or lead. Everything stalls behind it.
Use what you already built: your delivery map from Course 06, your SOPs from Course 09, your bench from Course 08.
Hand it off in stages. They shadow you, then you shadow them, then you only review, then you stop reviewing.
Quality holds because of the checklist and the standard, not because your hands are on it.
Your clients bought the outcome, not you doing the task. Deliver the outcome and they won't miss you in the work.
lessons.story: [STORY: the first job you didn't do yourself, and what it felt like to let it go]
lessons.action: Pick the delivery role you'll hand off first, name the person, and run the first shadow job this week.

lessons.title: Then sales
lessons.big_idea: Train someone to sell it like you do. Selling is a skill with a script, not a personality trait only you have.
talking_points: Sales comes second because you can't train someone to sell what you can't yet deliver without you.
Most owners think nobody can sell like them. That's usually because they never wrote down how they sell.
Give them the script, the objection sheet and recordings of your best calls from Course 05.
They listen to you, then they run calls while you listen, then they run calls alone and you review the recordings.
Pay on results. A base plus commission keeps the incentive where it belongs.
Watch the close rate, not the vibe. If the numbers hold, the handoff worked.
lessons.story: [STORY: training the first person to sell your offer — what you had to unlearn about thinking only you could do it]
lessons.action: Record your next three sales calls and build them into a training pack with your script and objection sheet.

lessons.title: Then management
lessons.big_idea: Hand over the operation. The last role to go is the one running the day, and it goes to a manager who holds your standard.
talking_points: Management is last because a manager needs systems to manage. Without delivery and sales handed off, there's nothing to run.
Your first manager is usually someone already on the team who holds the standard when you're not looking.
Hand them the keys in writing: what they decide alone, what they bring to you, and what they never touch.
They run the weekly meeting and own the scoreboard. You show up as a guest, then you stop showing up.
Your job changes to one weekly check on the numbers and one conversation with your manager.
If you keep stepping back in to fix things, you didn't hand over the operation. You loaned it.
lessons.action: Write the decision list for your manager: what they decide alone, what comes to you, and what is off limits.

lessons.title: Run it remote
lessons.big_idea: From your phone, from anywhere. If you can see the numbers and reach your manager, you can run the company.
talking_points: Running it remote isn't about where you sit. It's about whether the business needs you physically present to work.
Everything lives in the CRM. Every lead, client, job and dollar. If it's not in there, it doesn't exist.
Your phone holds three things: the scoreboard, the team channel and your calendar. That's the whole office.
Check the scoreboard daily. Talk to your manager weekly. Act only when a number moves the wrong way.
A national agency runs without me in the room. That only works because the system holds, not because I check in all day.
Test it. Run a week from somewhere else and write down every time you had to step in. Those are your next fixes.
lessons.story: A national agency runs without me in the room.
lessons.action: Run three working days entirely from your phone and log every moment you had to step in.

lessons.title: Walkthrough: how I handed a company to my brother
lessons.big_idea: Four steps — the work, the selling, the hiring, the operation. The same order you're running this week, done for real.
talking_points: I walked my brother from wanting a company to running one fully remote at six figures a month. This is how I handed it over.
Step one was the work. He learned to deliver it, then to get it delivered by someone else.
Step two was the selling. He learned the script and ran the calls until the numbers held without me.
Step three was the hiring. He learned to find good people, run paid trials and keep a bench.
Step four was the operation. The meetings, the scoreboard, the decisions. That's when it became his.
The order is the lesson. Skip a step and you end up back in the business.
lessons.story: I handed a company to my brother in four steps: the work, the selling, the hiring, the operation. [STORY: the details of each step — what was hardest for him, and the moment you knew it was his]
lessons.action: Mark where you are on the four steps — the work, the selling, the hiring, the operation — and write the next handoff on your calendar.

courses.assignment_walkthrough: Build your replacement map first: every role you hold, the hours it takes, who replaces you and a handoff date. Don't skip the hours column, because that's how you see which handoff buys back the most. Then hand off the first role this month, which for almost everyone is a piece of delivery. Good looks like a named person doing that role this month, with an SOP and a checklist, and you reviewing the result instead of doing the work. Post your map in the community.

courses.title: Scale
courses.intro: Scale is the same machine, bigger. You don't need ten new ideas. You need to find the one thing holding your growth and break it, then do it again.

lessons.title: Find the one constraint
lessons.big_idea: Your business only grows as fast as its tightest point. Find that one constraint and work on nothing else until it breaks.
talking_points: Every business has one constraint at a time. Not five. One.
Go back to the ten problems: leads, marketing, sales, retention, churn, recruiting, delegation, managing, leadership, scaling. Which one is yours right now?
Read your scoreboard. The constraint is the number that's flat while everything around it is ready to grow.
If you have more leads than you can close, it's sales. If you close more than you can deliver, it's delivery or hiring.
Fixing anything other than the constraint feels productive and changes nothing.
Break it, then look again. The constraint moves. That's how you know you're growing.
lessons.action: Name your one constraint in a sentence, with the number that proves it.

lessons.title: More clients, bigger clients, more per client
lessons.big_idea: There are only three ways to grow revenue. Pick the one your machine can handle right now.
talking_points: More clients means more leads and more closes. Your lead machine from Course 04 has to be running first.
Bigger clients means the same work for buyers with bigger budgets. Often it's the same hours for a bigger check.
More per client means more services, longer contracts, or a higher tier for the clients you already have.
More per client is usually the fastest. They already trust you. Clients who stay 12, 24, 38 months are worth far more than new ones.
Bigger clients is usually the most profitable. Value pricing scales with the size of the buyer.
Pick one of the three for the next 90 days. Doing all three at once is how you do none of them.
lessons.story: [STORY: the first time you went after a bigger client, and what changed in the offer or the price]
lessons.action: Pull your client list and write down which of the three levers would add the most revenue in 90 days, with the number.

lessons.title: Add offers
lessons.big_idea: Build the ladder. Give clients a next step up, so you're not starting from zero with every sale.
talking_points: A ladder is a set of offers in order, from the first yes to the biggest engagement.
The bottom rung is easy to say yes to. The top rung is where the money and the long contracts are.
Every new offer should use the same team, the same systems and the same buyers. If it needs a new machine, it's a new business.
Add one rung at a time. Prove it sells and delivers before you add the next.
Make the next step obvious. Every client should know what comes after the thing they bought.
More offers isn't the goal. A clear path up is.
lessons.action: Draw your ladder: what you sell now, one rung below it and one rung above it, with a price on each.

lessons.title: New markets, same machine
lessons.big_idea: Clone what works into the next niche. Same offer, same process, same team, new buyer.
talking_points: Once the machine works in one market, the cheapest growth is pointing it at another.
Pick a niche that buys the same outcome. The work barely changes. The language and the list do.
Rewrite the offer in their words, build a new list of 100 buyers, and run the same outreach.
Use a case study from your first market. Proof travels.
Don't change the delivery to fit the new market. If you have to rebuild the machine, it's the wrong market.
Run it as a test for 30 days. If the conversations come, scale it. If they don't, kill it and try the next niche.
lessons.story: Grove Central case study. [STORY: the first time you took what worked in one niche into another]
lessons.action: Pick one adjacent niche, rewrite your offer sentence for it, and build a list of 100 buyers in it.

lessons.title: Partnerships, equity and deals
lessons.big_idea: When to take a stake instead of a fee. A fee pays you once. Equity pays you when the thing you helped build grows.
talking_points: Once your machine produces real results for clients, the work itself becomes an asset you can trade.
Take a stake when you believe in the business, your work is a big driver of its growth, and you can afford to wait for the payoff.
Take the fee when the client can pay it, the upside is unclear, or you need the cash now.
A lot of the best deals are both: a reduced fee plus equity or a share of revenue.
Put everything in writing. Vesting, what you deliver, what happens if it ends. Get a lawyer on every equity deal.
Never let equity deals starve the core business of cash. The machine pays the bills first.
lessons.story: [STORY: a deal where you took or turned down a stake instead of a fee, and why]
lessons.action: List your current clients and partners, and mark any where a stake or revenue share would be worth more than the fee.

lessons.title: Build something you can sell
lessons.big_idea: Designing for an exit. A business you can sell is the same as a finished business, with the paperwork done.
talking_points: Even if you never sell, build it like you will. It makes the business better to own.
A buyer pays for three things: recurring revenue, a team that runs it without you, and clean numbers.
Recurring contracts beat one-off projects every time. That's why we put clients on contracts from Course 03.
If the business depends on you, a buyer is buying a job. Get out of the work first.
Clean books, written SOPs, a CRM with the full history. That's what makes a business something a buyer can trust.
Know what you'd want for it. A number on paper changes how you run it.
lessons.action: Score your business out of ten on recurring revenue, owner independence and clean numbers, and write the one fix for your lowest score.

lessons.title: The next level of you
lessons.big_idea: The person who can hold what you're building. The business grows to the size of the owner, so you grow first.
talking_points: Your business is a reflection of your standard. A bigger business needs a bigger standard.
The habits that got you here — doing it yourself, being in every decision — are what cap you now.
The next level is calmer, not busier. Fewer decisions, better ones.
Rich, Fit, Sick doesn't stop when the business grows. Train every day. Read. Hold the standard.
Spend time around people who are already where you're going. Your ceiling rises to the room.
Write down who you have to become to run the business you described. Then act like that person this week.
lessons.story: [STORY: a moment when you had to change yourself before the business could grow]
lessons.action: Write one paragraph on the person who can run the business you're building, and one habit you start this week to become them.

courses.assignment_walkthrough: Start with your scoreboard, not your gut. Name the one constraint in a sentence with the number that proves it, then pick one move that breaks it in the next 90 days. Good looks like: 'My constraint is sales — we get 40 leads a month and close 4. My move is hiring and training a closer by day 30.' One constraint, one move, one owner, one number. Post it in the community and bring it to the live call.

courses.title: The Life
courses.intro: This is the reason for everything we've done in the last eleven weeks. The business was never the point. The life it pays for is, so we're going to write it down and put it on the calendar.

lessons.title: Nobody actually wants a company
lessons.big_idea: You don't want a company. You want what a company gives you. Get clear on that, or you'll build a business that owns you.
talking_points: Nobody dreams about payroll and client calls. They dream about time, freedom, and the people they love.
The company is the vehicle. If you forget that, you'll keep building the vehicle and never go anywhere.
Ask yourself what you'd do with the company if it ran itself tomorrow. That answer is what you actually want.
Most owners who burn out built the business they thought they should, not the life they actually wanted.
Write the life first. Then make the business serve it.
If your business grew and your life didn't, you missed the point.
lessons.story: [STORY: the moment you realized the company was the vehicle, not the destination]
lessons.action: Write three sentences on what you actually want the business to give you, without mentioning the business.

lessons.title: Time freedom
lessons.big_idea: Time freedom is owning your calendar. You decide what goes on it, and the business doesn't need you to fill it.
talking_points: Time freedom isn't doing nothing. It's choosing what you do.
If you did the work in Course 07 and Course 12, you already bought back the hours. Now protect them.
Block the life first. Training, family, trips, deep work. Then the business gets what's left.
Keep your owner work to a fixed window. Scoreboard, manager check-in, the big decisions. That's it.
If your calendar is full of things someone else could do, you've given the time back to the business.
Free time fills up unless you design it. Protect it like a client meeting.
lessons.action: Build your ideal week on the calendar, with the life blocked in first and the business in a fixed window.

lessons.title: Location freedom
lessons.big_idea: Work from anywhere. If the business runs from your phone, where you live is a choice, not a constraint.
talking_points: Location freedom was designed in from day one. Remote team, CRM, scoreboard, phone.
A national agency runs without me in the room. That's what makes the room optional.
Start small. A long weekend away while the business runs. Then a week. Then longer.
Before you go, check the basics: your manager knows what they decide, the numbers are on your phone, and nothing waits on you.
Pay attention to what pulls you back in. Every one of those is a system to fix.
Pick where you want to be and go. The business should follow you, not hold you.
lessons.action: Choose a place you want to work from and book the dates.

lessons.title: Financial freedom
lessons.big_idea: Save, invest, and buy the life — not the number. Know what your life costs, then build the money to pay for it without you working.
talking_points: Most people chase a number. A number never feels like enough. A life does.
Start with what your life actually costs. The real one you wrote down, not a guess.
Pay yourself first, every month, from the business. Then save and invest a set amount before you spend.
Keep business money and personal money separate. You set that up in Course 11.
Build income that doesn't need you: the business running without you, and investments growing on their own.
Financial freedom is when what comes in without your time covers what your life costs. Work it backwards like any target.
lessons.action: Write what your life costs per month, and the amount you'll save and invest every month starting this month.

lessons.title: Health
lessons.big_idea: Train like it matters. It does. Your body is the one asset the business can't replace.
talking_points: Fit is in Rich, Fit, Sick for a reason. Train every day.
Your energy sets the pace for the whole company. A tired owner makes tired decisions.
Training is the first block on the calendar, not the one that gets moved when the day gets busy.
Sleep, food and training. Get those three right and most of the rest follows.
The Marine Corps taught me about showing up. That applies to your training as much as to your business.
There's no point building freedom you don't have the health to enjoy.
lessons.story: Marine Corps taught me about showing up. [STORY: what your training looks like now, and how you protect it]
lessons.action: Put your daily training on the calendar for the next 30 days and post your first week in the community.

lessons.title: Relationships
lessons.big_idea: The people you're building it for. If they don't get your time, the business took it.
talking_points: Most of us say we're building this for our family. Then we give them what's left after the business.
Write down the people who matter most. Then check how much of your week they actually get.
Be present when you're with them. The phone stays down. The business can wait an hour. It's built to.
Build it with the people close to you, not around them. Tell them what you're building and why.
The right people around you raise your standard. Choose them on purpose.
You can rebuild a business. You can't get back years you missed.
lessons.story: I walked my brother from wanting a company to running one fully remote at six figures a month. [STORY: what building with your brother meant to you beyond the business]
lessons.action: Name the three people who matter most and put one block of undistracted time with each of them on the calendar.

lessons.title: Give back
lessons.big_idea: Help the people coming up behind you. Teaching what you know is how you keep it, and how you pay it forward.
talking_points: Someone helped you get here. Now you're the one who can help.
Start in this room. Answer a question in the community. Share your numbers. Show your work.
Teach what you just learned. You understand it better once you've taught it.
Hire and train people. That's giving back too. I built my companies and trained the people who now run them. That's the most useful thing I know how to give.
Give your time, your money or your skills. Pick one and make it regular, not occasional.
A business that runs without you gives you the time to do this properly.
lessons.story: I trained the people who now run my companies. [STORY: someone who helped you when you were coming up]
lessons.action: Pick one person a stage behind you and help them this week, in the community or in real life.

courses.assignment_walkthrough: Write the life you're building toward in plain language: where you live, what your week looks like, who you spend it with, how you train, and what it costs per month. Keep it specific enough that you'd know when you're living it. Then put the first trip on the calendar with real dates, not 'sometime this year.' Good looks like a one-page description of your life and a booked trip, posted in the community.
